items.p: Which of these does a plant NOT need to grow well?
items.why: Plants need light, water, air, warmth and minerals. A seedling kept in the dark all day grows pale and weak. Picking 'air' usually means forgetting that roots and leaves breathe. Plants need air too.

items.p: A test where you change only one thing and keep everything else the same is called a ____ test.
items.why: In a fair test, only one thing is different, so you know what caused the result.

items.p: Look at the chart. The dark seedlings were taller. What else did you notice about them?
opts: They were pale, thin and floppy
items.why: In the dark, seedlings stretch tall to find light. They cannot make their green colour or food, so they are pale and weak. Picking 'greener' means thinking taller must be healthier.
items.context: This question is about the light test. You grow moong seedlings in 6 cups. Three get light and three are kept under a box, with everything else the same.

chart.title: The light test: middle height on Day 7 (made-up results)

items.p: In the light test, what is the one thing we change?
items.why: We change only the light. Everything else, like the seeds, soil and water, stays the same. Picking 'water' is a common slip. If water changed too, we couldn't tell which one made the difference.
items.context: This question is about the light test. You grow moong seedlings in 6 cups. Three get light and three are kept under a box, with everything else the same.

items.p: If you forget to water the dark cup in the light test, the test is still fair.
items.why: False. Then two things are different: light and water. You could not tell which one caused the result.
items.context: This question is about the light test. You grow moong seedlings in 6 cups. Three get light and three are kept under a box, with everything else the same.

items.p: Look at the chart. Which group grew best?
items.why: The JUST RIGHT group was tallest, at 13 cm. Picking SOAKED usually means thinking more water is always better. But soaked roots cannot breathe.
items.context: This question is about the water test. Three cups of moong get no water. Three get 2 teaspoons every second day. Three stand in a dish of water all the time.

chart.title: The water test: middle height on Day 14 (made-up results)

items.p: Why did the SOAKED seedlings turn yellow?
opts: Their roots could not get air, so they started to rot
items.why: Soaked soil has no air spaces left. Roots need air to breathe, so they rot. Picking 'too little water' is a mix-up: a yellow plant in soggy soil has too much water, not too little.
items.context: This question is about the water test. Three cups of moong get no water. Three get 2 teaspoons every second day. Three stand in a dish of water all the time.

items.p: When a plant droops and goes floppy because it needs water, we say it ____.
items.why: A wilting plant's cells are going soft, like balloons losing air.

items.p: Look at the chart. Where did the sprouts grow least?
items.why: In the cold fridge, the sprouts hardly grew: only 1 cm. Cold slows down the work of growing. Picking 'warm spot' means reading the shortest bar as the warmest place.
items.context: This question is about the warmth test. Moong sprouts are kept in the dark in a fridge, a room cupboard and a warm spot, and measured each day.

chart.title: The warmth test: growth of 5 sprouts in 3 days (made-up results)

items.p: Why did we cover all three bowls in the warmth test with plates?
opts: Because the fridge is dark, so all the bowls must be dark too
items.why: The inside of a fridge is dark. If only the fridge bowl was dark, light would change as well as warmth. Covering all three keeps light the same. Picking 'to keep them warm' misses that the plates are about light, not warmth.
items.context: This question is about the warmth test. Moong sprouts are kept in the dark in a fridge, a room cupboard and a warm spot, and measured each day.

items.p: Match each plant clue to the need that is missing.
pairs: Roots coming out of the hole
items.why: A plant's look tells you which need is missing. Leaning and pale means light. Drooping in dry soil means water. Yellow in soggy soil means the roots have no air. Roots out of the hole means it needs a bigger pot.

items.p: Sort these. Is it good care or bad care for a tulsi plant?
items: putting it on a sunny balcony
Good care
watering when the top of the soil is dry
Good care
standing the pot in a full bucket of water
Bad care
keeping it in a dark cupboard
Bad care
using a pot with a hole in the bottom
Good care
watering it five times a day
Bad care
items.why: Good care gives each need in the right amount. Too much water and too little light both harm a plant.

items.p: A moong seedling is 3 cm tall on Monday and 5 cm tall on Wednesday. How much did it grow?
items.why: 5 take away 3 is 2. So it grew 2 cm. Picking 8 means adding the two heights instead of finding the difference. Picking 5 gives its height, not its growth.

items.p: When you measure a seedling, the 0 on the ruler goes at the soil.
items.why: True. A plant's height is measured from the soil to its highest point.

items.p: Why do we test 3 cups of seedlings in the light and 3 in the dark, instead of just 1 of each?
items.a: Because one cup could be a fluke. For example, it might have bad seeds. With 3 cups we can see if they all do the same thing, and use the middle one.
items.why: Repeating a test makes the result more trustworthy.
items.context: This question is about the light test. You grow moong seedlings in 6 cups. Three get light and three are kept under a box, with everything else the same.

items.p: Name three things a plant needs. For each one, say what happens if it gets too little.
items.a: Light: it grows tall, pale and weak. Water: it wilts and dries up. Warmth: it grows very slowly. Any three needs with a correct result are right.
items.why: A good answer names a need and its effect, using what was seen in the tests.

items.p: Draw two seedlings: one grown in the light and one grown in the dark. Label the differences.
items.a: The light seedling is short, thick and green, with open leaves. The dark seedling is tall, thin, pale yellow and bent, with tiny closed leaves.
items.why: Drawing the differences shows that height is not the same as health.
items.art: An empty box split in two halves, labelled LIGHT and DARK.
items.context: This question is about the light test. You grow moong seedlings in 6 cups. Three get light and three are kept under a box, with everything else the same.

items.p: Riya wants to test if plants need light. Which test is fair?
opts: One pot in the sun with water, one pot in a cupboard with no water
Two pots of the same seedlings and soil, both watered the same, one in the sun and one in a cupboard
A big plant in the sun and a tiny plant in the cupboard
items.why: Only the light is different in this test. Picking the first one means missing that water changed too. Picking the third means missing that the plants were different sizes.

items.p: Look at the chart. The dark seedlings were 14 cm and the light ones were 8 cm. How much taller were the dark ones?
items.why: 14 take away 8 is 6. So the dark seedlings were 6 cm taller. Picking 22 means adding instead of finding the difference.
items.context: This question is about the light test. You grow moong seedlings in 6 cups. Three get light and three are kept under a box, with everything else the same.

chart.title: The light test: middle height on Day 7 (made-up results)

items.p: Dev measured three cups in the light: 8 cm, 9 cm and 8 cm. What is the middle value?
items.why: Put them in order: 8, 8, 9. The middle one is 8. Picking 25 means adding them all up. The middle value is one of the numbers, not their total.
items.context: This question is about the light test. You grow moong seedlings in 6 cups. Three get light and three are kept under a box, with everything else the same.

items.p: A yellow dark-grown seedling is put back on the windowsill. What usually happens in a day or two?
items.why: In the light, the seedling starts making green chlorophyll again. Picking 'dies at once' underestimates how quickly plants respond. It only dies if it stays in the dark until its stored food runs out.
items.context: This question is about the light test. You grow moong seedlings in 6 cups. Three get light and three are kept under a box, with everything else the same.

items.p: Rice grows standing in water in flooded fields. Why doesn't it drown, like our soaked moong?
opts: Rice has air channels that carry air down to its roots
The water in rice fields is special
items.why: Rice, lotus and mangroves all have ways to get air down to their roots. Moong does not. Picking 'rice doesn't need air' is a common guess. But all roots need air. Rice just has its own pipes for it.

items.p: Look at the chart. The fridge sprouts were then moved into the warm room. What most likely happened?
opts: They stayed the same, because they were dead
items.why: Cold slows growth down but does not kill moong sprouts quickly. In the warm, their helper molecules speed up again. Picking 'they were dead' mixes up 'not growing' with 'dead'.
items.context: This question is about the warmth test. Moong sprouts are kept in the dark in a fridge, a room cupboard and a warm spot, and measured each day.

chart.title: The warmth test: growth of 5 sprouts in 3 days (made-up results)

items.p: The hotter it is, the faster a plant always grows.
items.why: False. Warmth speeds growth up only to a point. Too much heat makes a plant lose water fast, and very high heat harms its helper molecules.

items.p: Wheat is sown in winter in Punjab. Rice is sown at the start of the monsoon. Why?
opts: Each crop has its own just-right warmth and water
Wheat seeds are only sold in winter
items.why: Wheat grows best in cool weather, and rice needs warmth and lots of water. Farmers match each crop to its season. Picking a reason about selling or being busy misses that it is about what each plant needs.

items.p: Is this a need a plant has, or something it can live without?
items: light
A need
soil itself
Can live without
water
A need
music
Can live without
air for its roots
A need
minerals
A need
items.why: Plants need light, water, air and minerals. They do not need soil itself, only what it gives. A money plant grows in a jar of water. Music has not been shown to help.

items.p: Growing plants with their roots in water mixed with minerals, and no soil, is called ____.
items.why: Hydroponic farms grow lettuce and herbs this way, on rooftops and even in space.

items.p: Zoya's moong grew very tall but pale, with folded leaves, in a dim window. What was its shortest plank, the need in shortest supply?
items.why: Tall, pale and leaning are the clues of too little light. Picking 'water' is common, but a thirsty plant droops in dry soil. It does not grow tall and pale.
items.context: This question is about the story A Stripe of Sun. Zoya grew moong on a windowsill facing a wall. Her narrow lane got sun for only a short time each day.

items.p: Someone says: 'My plant grows well because I talk to it.' What is the best question to ask?
opts: What do you say to it?
Did you also water and check it more than your other plants?
items.why: Talking usually comes with more care, so more than one thing changes. That makes it an unfair test. Picking 'what do you say' assumes talking is the cause before testing it.

items.p: Put the steps of the light test in order.
items: Sow 5 moong in each of 6 cups
Cover 3 cups with a box
Water every cup the same every second day
Measure the tallest seedling in each cup
Draw a bar chart and write a conclusion
items.why: First you set up the cups. Then you change the one thing. Then you care for them all the same way and measure. Last, you show and explain your results.
items.context: This question is about the light test. You grow moong seedlings in 6 cups. Three get light and three are kept under a box, with everything else the same.

items.p: A cactus is watered every day and its stem goes soft and black. What happened?
opts: Its roots rotted from too much water, because a cactus needs very little
items.why: A cactus comes from dry places and needs only a little water. Daily watering drowns its roots. Picking 'too little water' means using one rule for every plant. Each plant has its own just right.

items.p: Gokhale Kaka said the tallest plant would win. In the story, why was that a bad way to choose the healthiest plant? What would you measure instead?
items.a: The tallest plant was tall because it was starving for light and stretching. It was pale and weak. I would also count the green leaves, look at the colour, and check if the stem is strong.
items.why: Height alone can be misleading. Good scientists choose what to measure carefully.
items.context: This question is about the story A Stripe of Sun. In a building in Mumbai, children had a contest to grow the tallest moong. Zoya's moong, in a dim window, grew tallest but was pale and fell over.

items.p: Plan a fair test to find out if methi grows better in sunlight or in a shady corner. Say what you will change, what you will keep the same, and what you will measure.
items.a: I will change only the place: one group of methi cups in the sun and one in the shade. I will keep the same seeds, soil, cups and water. I will measure the height of the tallest seedling in each cup every two days, and count the green leaves.
items.why: A good plan names one thing to change, several things to keep the same, and one thing to measure.

items.p: Draw a bar chart for these heights: NONE 5 cm, JUST RIGHT 13 cm, SOAKED 8 cm. Label both lines.
items.a: Three bars. NONE is 5 squares tall, JUST RIGHT 13 squares and SOAKED 8 squares. The bottom line says 'Group' and the side line says 'Height (cm)'.
items.why: A bar chart shows at a glance which group grew best.
items.art: Empty squared graph paper with a bottom line and a side line numbered 0 to 15.
items.context: This question is about the water test. Three cups of moong get no water. Three get 2 teaspoons every second day. Three stand in a dish of water all the time.

worksheets.title: Just Right, Deep Down and in Space (challenge)

items.p: In the warmth test, the warm spot at 33 °C gave the most growth. Could you say that moong grows best at the hottest place possible?
opts: No. We only tested three temperatures. Above a certain point, heat harms plants
Yes, because the warm bar was tallest
items.why: We did not test hotter places, so we cannot say what happens there. Other experiments show that great heat harms plants. Picking 'the hotter the better' stretches the result beyond what was tested. Good scientists only claim what their test showed.
items.context: This question is about the warmth test. Moong sprouts are kept in the dark in a fridge, a room cupboard and a warm spot, and measured each day.

chart.title: The warmth test: growth of 5 sprouts in 3 days (made-up results)

items.p: Under green cellophane, seedlings often grow taller and paler, as in dim light. Why?
opts: Leaves use red and blue light most and bounce back much of the green, so they get less of the light they use
items.why: A leaf looks green because it reflects more green light than other colours. So green light is the colour it uses least. Picking 'cold colour' mixes up how colours feel to us with what plants use.
items.context: This question is about the coloured light test. Four cups of seedlings are covered with clear, red, blue or green see-through cellophane for a week.

items.p: A plant in a dark corner gets extra fertiliser but grows no better. What does this show?
opts: Its growth was held back by its scarcest need, light, so more minerals did not help
items.why: This is the idea of the shortest plank. Extra of one need does not help if another need is in short supply. Picking 'fertiliser never works' stretches one result to every case.

items.p: Who first published the idea that a plant grows only as well as its scarcest need allows?
items.why: Carl Sprengel published it in 1828. Liebig made it famous later, so it was often called Liebig's law. Picking Liebig is what many old textbooks say.

items.p: A seedling under a brick knows it is dark. What does it use to sense light?
opts: Special light-sensing molecules called photoreceptors, such as phytochrome
It can't sense light at all
items.why: Plants have no eyes, but special molecules flip like switches in light. Picking 'can't sense light' misses that seedlings clearly change how they grow in the dark.

items.p: Scientists have found that one light-sensing molecule in plants, phytochrome B, also changes faster when it is warm.
items.why: True. In 2016, two teams found that phytochrome B also acts like a thermometer. Plants seem to have other warmth sensors too, and scientists are still working out how they all fit together.

items.p: Cotton sprouted on the far side of the Moon in January 2019, inside a sealed can on the Chang'e 4 spacecraft. Why did the experiment end soon after?
opts: The freezing Moon night came, and it got far too cold
items.why: A night on the Moon lasts about two Earth weeks and is extremely cold. Warmth is a need. Picking 'too much water' misses that the big problem on the Moon is the cold.
items.context: Chang'e 4 is a Chinese spacecraft that landed on the far side of the Moon in January 2019. It carried a small sealed can with seeds, soil, water and air.

items.p: Plants on the International Space Station grow under pink-purple lamps. Why those colours?
opts: They are a mix of red and blue, the colours of light plants use most
Plants in space prefer dark colours
items.why: The lamps mix red and blue, the colours leaves use most. Picking 'they look nice' misses that the colour was chosen for the plants, not for us.

items.p: Why does warmth make a sprout grow faster, deep down?
opts: Warm molecules jiggle faster and bump more, so the plant's helper molecules work faster
Heat is a kind of food
items.why: Temperature is how fast molecules jiggle. Faster jiggling means more bumps each second, so the work of growing goes faster. Picking 'heat is food' mixes up energy for warmth with food. The sprout's food is stored in the seed.

items.p: Why can very great heat harm a plant, even if it has water?
opts: Its helper molecules unfold and stop working, like egg white turning solid when cooked
Heat makes the plant too heavy
Heat turns the leaves into sugar
items.why: Enzymes are folded into special shapes. Too much heat shakes them out of shape, and they stop working. Picking 'too heavy' has nothing to do with heat. This unfolding is like cooking an egg.

items.p: Match each person to what they found out about plants and their needs.
pairs: built the crescograph, which showed growth changing from minute to minute
first published the idea of the scarcest need, in 1828
grew plants in mineral water with no soil, in the 1860s
found plants respond to the vibrations of caterpillars chewing
items.why: Each of these scientists tested an idea about what plants need or sense.

items.p: A plant that is talked to every day and grows well proves that talking helps plants grow.
items.why: False. The talked-to plant probably also got more care and checking. Only a fair test, with the same care for both groups, could show it.

items.p: Bose's growth magnifier made the plant's growth look 4 times bigger. The pointer moved 20 millimetres in 2 hours. How much did the plant grow in those 2 hours, and how much in one hour?
items.a: 20 divided by 4 is 5. So the plant grew 5 millimetres in 2 hours. That is 2 and a half millimetres each hour.
items.why: Divide the pointer's movement by how much the lever magnifies, then share it between the hours.
items.context: In the growth magnifier activity, a straw lever is tied to the top of a growing plant. The long end of the straw moves 4 times as far as the plant grows.

items.p: In the light test, we kept some seedlings in the dark until they were weak. Is that fair to the seedlings? Give one reason for and one reason against.
items.a: For: we learnt something important about plants. We put the dark seedlings back in the light at the end, and most turned green again. Against: we made living things suffer on purpose. Any answer with a reason on each side is good.
items.why: There is no single right answer. The point is to think about both sides.

items.p: Astronauts plan to grow food on the Moon. List what the plants need, and say where the astronauts could get each one.
items.a: Light: from the Sun in the long Moon day, or from lamps. Water: brought from Earth, or from ice found near the Moon's poles. Air: made and pumped in a sealed greenhouse. Warmth: heaters and insulation, because Moon nights are freezing. Minerals: from Moon soil with extra added.
items.why: A good answer covers every need from this unit, and notices that Earth gives most of them for free.

items.p: A friend's fern on a sunny terrace has brown, crispy edges, and a friend's cactus in a dark bathroom is pale and leaning. Give each one a diagnosis and a cure.
items.a: The fern has too much sun and heat. Move it to a shadier, cooler place and keep it damp. The cactus has too little light. Move it to a sunny window and water it only a little.
items.why: Each kind of plant has its own just right. The same place can be too much for one plant and too little for another.

items.p: Draw the shortest-plank bucket for Zoya's moong in the dim window. Label each plank with a need, and make the shortest plank the need that held it back.
items.a: A bucket with planks for light, water, air, warmth and minerals. The light plank is the shortest, and water spills out over it.
items.why: Zoya's moong had water, air, warmth and soil, but very little light. So light was its shortest plank.
items.art: An outline of a wooden bucket with five empty planks to label.
items.context: This question is about the story A Stripe of Sun. Zoya grew moong in a dim window facing a wall. It had water and soil but very little sun.

experiments.title: The Light Test: what happens in the dark?
experiments.question: Do moong seedlings need light to grow well? What happens to them in the dark?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After a week, will the seedlings in the dark be taller or shorter than the ones in the light? Will they be green or another colour? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: Change only the light. Use 6 cups that are the same, the same soil, and 5 moong seeds in each cup. Put all 6 cups side by side near the same window. Cover 3 of them with a cardboard box. Water every cup with the same spoonful at the same time. Measure every cup at the same time of day. We use 3 cups for each, because one cup could be a fluke.
results_table: Day 3: height of the tallest seedling (cm)

materials.item: 6 small paper cups or yoghurt cups, each with a small hole poked in the bottom
soil from a garden or a nursery, enough to fill the cups
30 moong seeds, soaked in water overnight
a cardboard box big enough to cover 3 cups and keep out all light
a tray or old plate to stand the cups on
a teaspoon for watering
a 30 cm ruler
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: A grown-up pokes the holes in the cups. Wash hands after touching soil. Do not eat the seeds.

schedule.what: Sow 5 soaked moong in each of 6 cups. Write your prediction. Put 3 cups under the box and 3 beside it in the light.
Water every cup with 2 teaspoons. Put the box back quickly.
Water and measure the tallest seedling in each cup. Write the heights and colours.
Water every cup the same.
Water and measure again.
Water every cup the same.
Measure, count the green leaves, compare and draw a bar chart. Say what you think, what you saw and why.
Put the dark cups in the light. Look again tomorrow. Do they turn green?

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw two bar charts: one of the heights on Day 7, and one of the number of open green leaves.

flow.do: 1. Put the soaked moong in a bowl. 2. Ask your child to predict what will happen in the dark, and write it down.
flow.say: Some seedlings will grow in the light, and some in the dark. In a week, which do you think will be taller? Which will be greener?
flow.kid: Some moong will grow in the light. Some will grow in the dark. Guess: which will be taller? Which will be greener? Write it down.

ask.q: Why do you think that?
good: Plants need light, so the dark ones will be small.
They might grow up to look for light.

flow.parent: Most children predict the dark seedlings will be smaller. That is a fine prediction. The surprise is part of the lesson.
flow.context: This is the first step of the light test. You grow moong seedlings in the light and in the dark, and keep everything else the same.

flow.do: 1. Fill 6 cups with soil to about one finger-width below the rim. 2. Press 5 soaked moong into each cup, about as deep as your fingernail. 3. Water each cup with 2 teaspoons. 4. Label 3 cups LIGHT and 3 cups DARK. 5. Stand all 6 on a tray near a bright window. 6. Cover the 3 DARK cups with the box.
flow.say: We'll keep everything the same except one thing. Same cups, same soil, same seeds, same water, same window. The only difference is the box.
flow.kid: Fill 6 cups with soil. Push 5 moong into each one. Give each cup 2 spoons of water. Put a box over 3 cups. Everything else stays the same.

ask.q: What is the one thing we are changing?
good: Whether the cup is under the box.

ask.q: What are we keeping the same?
good: The soil, the seeds, the cups, the water, the window.

flow.do: Every second day, lift the box for as short a time as you can. Water every cup with the same 2 teaspoons. Put the box back straight away.
flow.say: We lift the box quickly, so the dark cups get as little light as possible. And every cup gets exactly the same water.
flow.kid: Lift the box. Give every cup 2 spoons of water. Put the box back fast. The dark cups must stay dark.
flow.wait: Water every 2 days. Measure on Day 3 and Day 5.

flow.do: On Day 3 and Day 5: 1. Find the tallest seedling in each cup. 2. Stand the ruler on the soil beside it, with the 0 at the soil. 3. Read the number at the highest point of the seedling. 4. Write the height and the colour in the table.
flow.say: Put the zero of the ruler right at the soil. Read the number at the very top of the tallest seedling.
flow.kid: Stand the ruler on the soil. Zero goes at the bottom. Read the number at the top of the tallest seedling. Write it down.
flow.parent: Dark seedlings often grow with a hooked top. Measure to the highest point, not along the bend. If your child finds it hard to read the small marks, round to the nearest centimetre for now.

check.q: Where should the 0 on the ruler go when you measure a seedling?
options: At the top of the cup
At the end of the ruler, wherever it is
check.why: The height of a plant is measured from the soil to its top. So the 0 goes at the soil. Picking 'the top of the cup' is a common slip. Then the part of the stem inside the cup is not counted.

flow.do: On Day 7: 1. Take the box off. 2. Line up all 6 cups. 3. Measure the tallest seedling in each cup. 4. Count the open green leaves in each cup. 5. Look closely at the stems and colours.
flow.say: Let's look at all of them together. Which are taller? Which are greener? Which are stronger?
flow.kid: Take the box off. Line up all the cups. Measure each one. Count the open green leaves. What do you notice?

ask.q: What do the dark seedlings look like?
good: Their leaves are tiny and closed.

ask.q: Was your prediction right?

flow.parent: Usually the dark seedlings are taller, but yellow or white, thin and floppy, with small folded leaves. The light seedlings are shorter, thicker and green, with open leaves. This surprises most children.

check.q: The dark seedlings grew taller than the light seedlings. Does that mean they are healthier?
options: No. They are tall because they are stretching to find light, and they are pale and weak
check.why: In the dark, a seedling uses its stored food to grow tall and thin, looking for light. It cannot make green chlorophyll or new food. So it is weak and will die when its stored food runs out. Picking 'taller means healthier' is the most common idea. That is why we also count the green leaves.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table on Day 7

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart of the Day 7 heights. Use the middle height of the 3 LIGHT cups and of the 3 DARK cups.
flow.say: To find the middle height, put the 3 numbers in order and take the middle one. Then draw one bar for LIGHT and one for DARK.
flow.kid: Put the 3 LIGHT heights in order. The middle one is your LIGHT bar. Do the same for DARK. Draw both bars.
flow.parent: With the made-up numbers, LIGHT is 8, 8, 9, so the middle is 8. DARK is 13, 14, 15, so the middle is 14. Using the middle value stops one odd cup from fooling us.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: plants need light to grow well. What I saw: the dark seedlings were 14 cm tall but yellow and floppy, with no open green leaves. The light ones were 8 cm, green and strong. Why: without light they could not make food or green colour. So they used their stored food to stretch up and look for light.

flow.do: On Day 8, move the dark cups into the light. Look again the next day.
flow.say: Let's give the dark seedlings their light back. What do you think will happen by tomorrow?
flow.kid: Put the dark cups in the light. Look tomorrow. Do they turn green?
flow.parent: Within a day or two, the yellow seedlings usually turn green, because they start making chlorophyll in the light. It is a kind way to end the test, too.
flow.think: The dark seedlings had no eyes. How did they know they were in the dark?

experiments.title: The Water Test: too little, just right, too much
experiments.question: How much water do moong seedlings need? Is more water always better?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which cups will do best: no water, just right water, or soaked all the time? Which will do worst? Write your guesses and reasons.
experiments.fair_test: Change only the water. Grow all 9 cups of seedlings the same way for 5 days first. Then give 3 cups no water and 3 cups 2 teaspoons every second day. Stand the last 3 cups in a dish that is always full of water. Keep the cups side by side on the same windowsill. Measure every cup at the same time of day.
results_table: Leaves: firm, drooping, yellow or dry?

materials.item: 9 small paper cups or yoghurt cups, each with a small hole poked in the bottom
soil from a garden or a nursery
45 moong seeds, soaked overnight
2 trays or old plates, and 1 deep dish or a cut-off plastic bottle bottom
a teaspoon for watering
a 30 cm ruler
labels: NONE, JUST RIGHT, SOAKED

experiments.safety: A grown-up pokes the holes in the cups. Wash hands after touching soil. Throw away soggy, smelly soil outside, not in the kitchen.

schedule.what: Sow 5 soaked moong in each of 9 cups. Water all cups the same and put them on the windowsill.
Water all 9 cups the same.
Measure all cups. Write your predictions. Start the three treatments: none, just right, soaked.
Water the JUST RIGHT cups. Top up the SOAKED dish. Write one line about each group.
Water, top up and measure.
Water, top up and look closely at the leaves.
Final measuring. Tip one cup from each group out to look at the roots. Draw a bar chart and say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar chart of the middle height of each group on Day 14. Draw what the roots looked like in each group.

flow.do: 1. Fill 9 cups with soil. 2. Press 5 soaked moong into each. 3. Water each cup with 2 teaspoons. 4. Put all 9 on a tray on a bright windowsill.
flow.say: First we grow all 9 cups exactly the same way, so they start the test the same.
flow.kid: Fill 9 cups with soil. Push 5 moong into each. Give each 2 spoons of water. Put them all on the windowsill.
flow.wait: Let the seedlings grow for 5 days. Water all 9 cups the same, 2 teaspoons every second day.
flow.context: This is the first step of the water test. You grow 9 cups of moong seedlings, then give some no water, some just the right amount and some far too much.

flow.do: On Day 6: 1. Measure the tallest seedling in each cup and write it down. 2. Label 3 cups NONE, 3 JUST RIGHT and 3 SOAKED. 3. Stand the 3 SOAKED cups in a deep dish and fill it with water up to halfway up the cups. 4. Put all the cups back side by side.
flow.say: Now the test begins. These get no water at all. These get 2 spoons every second day. And these stand in water all the time. Which do you think will do best?
flow.kid: Measure every cup. Put labels on: NONE, JUST RIGHT, SOAKED. Stand the SOAKED cups in a dish of water. Which will do best? Guess.

ask.q: Which do you think will do best? Why?
good: Just right, because too much is bad too.

flow.parent: Many children predict the soaked cups will do best. Let them. The test will answer it.

flow.do: Every second day: 1. Water the JUST RIGHT cups with 2 teaspoons. 2. Top up the dish under the SOAKED cups. 3. Give the NONE cups nothing. 4. Press a finger into the soil of one cup from each group and write: dry, damp or soggy.
flow.say: Feel the soil. Dry, damp or soggy? Write it down for each group.
flow.kid: Water only the JUST RIGHT cups. Top up the dish. Feel the soil in each group. Dry, damp or soggy? Write it down.

flow.do: On Day 8 or 10, look closely at the leaves in each group together.
flow.say: Let's be plant doctors. What do the leaves look like in each group?
flow.kid: Look at the leaves in each group. Are they firm, drooping, yellow or dry?

check.q: The NONE cups have drooping, floppy leaves. What is the plant telling us?
check.why: A plant that droops in dry soil is wilting. Its cells are going soft because there is not enough water to fill them. Picking 'light' is a sensible guess, because plants in the dark also flop. But in the dark they are pale and tall. These are green and drooping, and their soil is dry.

flow.do: On Day 14: 1. Measure the tallest seedling in each cup. 2. Gently tip one cup from each group onto newspaper. 3. Wash the soil off the roots in a bowl of water. 4. Compare the roots.
flow.say: Let's look at the hidden part, the roots. What do the roots look like in each group?
flow.kid: Measure every cup. Then tip out one cup from each group. Wash the roots gently. Compare them.

ask.q: What do the SOAKED roots look like?
What do the JUST RIGHT roots look like?

flow.parent: Usually: NONE seedlings are dried up and brown, with thin dry roots. JUST RIGHT seedlings are green and firm, with white, spreading roots. SOAKED seedlings are often yellowing and shorter, with brown, soft roots. In some weather the soaked cups survive for longer. That is real science too. Write down what you actually saw.

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart of the middle height in each group on Day 14.
flow.say: One bar for each group. Put the three heights in order and use the middle one.
flow.kid: Draw a bar for NONE, JUST RIGHT and SOAKED. Use the middle height of each group.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.

What I saw: the JUST RIGHT seedlings were 13 cm and green. The NONE ones dried up, and the SOAKED ones were 8 cm and yellow with brown roots. Why: without water the cells go soft. In soaked soil the roots cannot get air, so they rot.
flow.think: Rice grows standing in water. Why doesn't it drown like our moong? (Hint: rice has air channels that carry air down to its roots.)

experiments.context: This is the water test. You grow 9 cups of moong seedlings the same way. Then 3 cups get no water, 3 get just the right amount and 3 get far too much. You measure and compare them.

experiments.title: The Warmth Test: cold, cool or warm?
experiments.question: Do moong sprouts grow faster when they are warm or when they are cold?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Some sprouts go in the fridge, some in a room cupboard and some in a warm spot. After 3 days, which will have grown longest? Write your guess and reason.
experiments.fair_test: Change only the warmth. Use 3 steel katoris or bowls that are the same, each with the same wet cotton and 10 sprouts. The fridge is dark inside, so cover all 3 bowls with a plate to make them all dark. Put the same amount of water in each. Measure all three at the same time each day.

materials.item: about 40 moong seeds, soaked overnight and left on a wet cloth for 1 day until tiny roots show
3 steel katoris or small bowls of the same size, and 3 plates to cover them
cotton wool
a teaspoon
a room thermometer, if you have one
a 30 cm ruler

experiments.safety: For the warm spot, use the top of the fridge at the back, or a closed cupboard in a warm room. Never use the stove, the oven, a heater or a flame. Do not eat the sprouts afterwards.

schedule.what: Set up the three bowls. Measure the sprouts. Put one bowl in the fridge, one in a room cupboard and one in a warm spot.
Measure the 5 longest sprouts in each bowl. Read the temperature in each place.
Measure again.
Final measuring. Work out how much each bowl grew. Draw a bar chart. Move the fridge bowl into the room and watch.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. For each place, take the first total away from the last total. Draw one bar for each place.

flow.do: Show your child the sprouted moong and ask for a prediction.
flow.say: We'll keep some sprouts cold, some cool and some warm. Which do you think will grow the most in 3 days?
flow.kid: Some sprouts go in the fridge. Some go in a cupboard. Some go somewhere warm. Guess: which will grow most?
flow.context: This is the first step of the warmth test. You keep moong sprouts in a cold, a cool and a warm place, in the dark, and measure how much they grow.

flow.do: 1. Put a flat layer of cotton in each bowl. 2. Wet each with exactly 4 teaspoons of water. 3. Put 10 sprouts on the cotton in each bowl. 4. Measure the 5 longest sprouts in each bowl, from the tip of the root to the top, and add them up. 5. Cover each bowl with a plate.
flow.say: The fridge is dark inside. So we cover all three bowls with a plate, to make them all dark. That way only the warmth is different.
flow.kid: Put cotton in 3 bowls. Wet each with 4 spoons of water. Put 10 sprouts in each. Measure 5 sprouts. Cover each bowl with a plate.

ask.q: Why do we cover all three bowls, not just the fridge one?
good: So only the warmth is different.

flow.parent: Adding up 5 sprouts gives one number for each bowl, and evens out small and big sprouts. A sprout that is 2 cm, 3 cm, 2 cm, 3 cm and 2 cm adds up to 12 cm.

flow.do: 1. Put one bowl in the fridge, not the freezer. 2. Put one bowl in a cupboard in a room. 3. Put one bowl in a warm spot, like the top of the fridge at the back. 4. If you have a thermometer, leave it in each place for 5 minutes and read it.
flow.say: Let's read the temperature in each place. The fridge is about 5 degrees. A room in India is often between 25 and 32 degrees.
flow.kid: Put one bowl in the fridge. Put one in a cupboard. Put one somewhere warm. Read the thermometer in each place.
flow.parent: Never use the stove, oven, a heater or a flame for the warm spot. Top of the fridge, a cupboard near a sunny wall, or a closed box in a warm room is enough. In winter, the warm spot matters more.

flow.do: On Day 2 and Day 3: take each bowl out, measure the 5 longest sprouts and add them up. Add 1 teaspoon of water if the cotton is drying. Put each bowl back quickly.
flow.say: Measure the 5 longest sprouts and add them up. Which bowl is growing fastest?
flow.kid: Measure the 5 longest sprouts in each bowl. Add them up. Write the total. Put the bowl back fast.

check.q: You add water to the warm bowl because its cotton is drying. What should you do for the other two bowls?
options: Add the same amount, so the water stays the same in all three
check.why: In a fair test, only the warmth should be different. If one bowl gets more water, water changes too. Picking 'nothing' usually means thinking only about the bowl in front of you, and not about keeping the test fair.

flow.do: On Day 4: 1. Measure one last time. 2. For each bowl, take the Day 1 total away from the last total. That is how much it grew. 3. Draw a bar for each place.
flow.say: Take the first total away from the last total. That tells us how much each bowl grew. Let's draw one bar for each.
flow.kid: Take the first number away from the last number. That is how much it grew. Draw one bar for each place.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: moong sprouts grow faster when they are warm. What I saw: in 3 days the fridge sprouts grew 1 cm. The cupboard ones grew 18 cm and the warm ones 24 cm. Why: warmth makes the tiny helpers inside the sprouts work faster.

flow.do: Move the fridge bowl into the room cupboard. Look again in 2 days.
flow.say: Are the fridge sprouts dead, or only waiting? Let's warm them up and see.
flow.kid: Put the fridge bowl in the cupboard. Look in 2 days. Are the sprouts dead, or only waiting?
flow.parent: The cold sprouts usually start growing again in the warmth. Cold slowed them down. It did not kill them.
flow.think: Our warm spot was best. Would an even hotter place, like a terrace at 46 degrees, be even better? Why not?

experiments.context: This is the warmth test. You put moong sprouts in a fridge, a room cupboard and a warm spot, all in the dark. You measure how much they grow in 3 days.

experiments.title: Coloured Light: does the colour matter?
experiments.question: Do seedlings grow differently under red, blue, green or clear see-through covers?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which colour of light will grow the greenest, strongest seedlings? Which will grow the weakest? Plants are green. Do you think they like green light best?
experiments.fair_test: Change only the colour of the cover. Use 4 cups of seedlings sown on the same day, the same soil and the same water. Make 4 cone-shaped covers of the same size, from clear, red, blue and green cellophane. Stand the cups side by side in the same bright place.

materials.item: 4 cups of moong seedlings, sown on the same day and about 2 cm tall
cellophane sheets: clear, red, blue and green
sticky tape and 4 thin sticks or straws to hold the covers up
a 30 cm ruler

experiments.safety: Leave a small gap at the bottom of each cover so air can get in. Do not leave the cups in hot afternoon sun, because the covers can trap heat.

schedule.what: Make 4 cellophane covers and put one over each cup. Write your predictions.
Water every cup the same and look through the covers.
Take off the covers. Measure, compare colour and leaves, and say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw each seedling in its colour of light.

flow.do: 1. Push 4 sticks or straws into the soil around each cup's edge. 2. Roll a sheet of cellophane into a tall cone or tube and tape it to the sticks. 3. Leave a small gap at the bottom for air. 4. Use one colour for each cup: clear, red, blue, green.
flow.say: Each cup gets a coloured window. The clear one lets all the colours of sunlight through. The others let mostly one colour through.
flow.kid: Make a tall see-through hat for each cup. One clear, one red, one blue, one green. Leave a gap at the bottom for air.
flow.context: This is the first step of the coloured light test. You cover cups of seedlings with clear, red, blue and green see-through sheets and see how they grow.

ask.q: Plants are green. Which colour do you think they like best?
good: Maybe not green. Maybe they bounce green light away.

flow.do: Every 3 days, lift each cover for a moment, water each cup with the same 2 teaspoons and put the cover back.
flow.say: Same water for every cup. Only the colour is different.
flow.kid: Lift each hat. Give each cup 2 spoons of water. Put the hat back.
flow.wait: Water every 3 days. Look on Day 7.

flow.do: On Day 7: 1. Take off the covers. 2. Measure the tallest seedling in each cup. 3. Compare leaf colour, stem thickness and how much each seedling leans.
flow.say: Which seedlings look most like the ones in full light? Which look most like the ones in the dark?
flow.kid: Take off the hats. Measure each cup. Which seedlings are greenest and strongest? Which look like they were in the dark?
flow.parent: Often the clear and red cups look healthiest, and blue gives short green seedlings. Green often looks a bit like the dark cups, taller and paler. Results at home vary. Cellophane sheets also let different amounts of light through, so this test is not perfectly fair. That is worth talking about.

check.q: Plants are green because their leaves bounce back much of the green light. So, under green cellophane, what do the seedlings mostly get?
options: The light they use least, so they grow as if in dim light
check.why: A leaf looks green because it uses red and blue light most and bounces back more green light. Under green cellophane, the seedlings get mostly the colour they use least. So they often stretch and stay pale, as in dim light. Picking 'the light they use best' is a very common guess, because plants are green.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why. Then talk about what made the test less than perfectly fair.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you see? Why? And was our test perfectly fair?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why. Then think: was the test perfectly fair?
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: plants use some colours of light better than others. What I saw: under green, the seedlings were taller and paler than under clear or red. Why: plants bounce back green light, so they get less of the light they use. The test was not perfectly fair, because the coloured sheets let different amounts of light through.
flow.think: Astronauts grow lettuce under red and blue lamps, which make a pink glow. Why not plain green lamps?

experiments.context: This is the coloured light test. You cover 4 cups of seedlings with clear, red, blue and green see-through sheets, and compare how they grow after a week. It is based on an idea in the founder's notes: compare plant growth under different colours of light.

example_chart.note: These numbers are made up. Height alone does not tell the whole story: the green cup's seedlings were also pale.

activities.title: The Grass Under the Brick

materials.item: a brick, a flat stone, a flowerpot or an old doormat
a patch of grass or weeds, in a park, a garden or a crack in the pavement
a notebook and pencil

activities.safety: Go outside only with a grown-up. Lift stones carefully and look before you touch, in case an insect or a scorpion is hiding underneath.

schedule.what: Lift something that has lain on grass for a long time. Notice and wonder.
Lift the brick you put down a week ago. Has the grass changed?

activities.record: Draw the grass under the brick and the grass beside it. Write three things you notice and one thing you wonder.

flow.do: Find something that has lain on grass or weeds for a while: a brick, a pot, a mat, a plank. Lift it together and look.
flow.say: Let's look under here. What do you notice about the grass? Don't explain yet. Just notice.
flow.kid: Lift the brick with a grown-up. Look at the grass underneath. What do you notice?

ask.q: What do you notice?
What do you wonder?

flow.parent: Do not explain yet. The light test will answer the question. Write down your child's wonderings, so you can come back to them.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Grass Under the Brick. It is a way into the unit: something real to notice before any explaining.

flow.do: If you can, put a brick or a flat stone on a patch of green grass that you can visit again. Mark the day.
flow.say: Let's do our own test. We'll put a brick here on green grass and look again in a week.
flow.kid: Put a brick on some green grass. Remember where. You will look again in a week.

ask.q: What do you predict we'll find in a week?

flow.do: A week later, lift the brick again and compare.
flow.say: Was your prediction right? What was the only thing the brick took away from the grass?
flow.kid: Lift the brick. Is the grass yellow now? What did the brick take away?

check.q: Under the brick, the grass still had water, air and soil. What did the brick take away?
check.why: The brick blocked the light. The grass still got rain from around the brick, and air from the soil. Without light, grass cannot make its green colour, so it goes pale. Picking 'water' or 'air' is a sensible guess. But the soil under a brick is usually damp, and the grass was still alive.

flow.think: Put the brick back somewhere else. In a few days, does the yellow patch turn green again?

activities.context: This is a short noticing activity to start the unit. You lift a brick that has lain on grass and look at what happened to the grass underneath.

activities.title: Measure Like a Scientist: the paper-strip growth chart

materials.item: a 30 cm ruler with millimetre marks
a growing plant, such as a seedling from the light test or a bean plant
a long strip of paper about 2 cm wide, scissors and glue
a big sheet of paper or a notebook page

schedule.what: Practise measuring things in centimetres and millimetres. Measure the plant and cut and stick the first strip.
Measure, cut a strip and stick it next to yesterday's.
After 10 days of strips, look at the chart. Which day did it grow most?

activities.record: A row of paper strips, one for each day, each as long as the plant was tall that day. Write the date and the height under each strip.

flow.do: 1. Look at the ruler together: find 0, the big numbered centimetre lines and the tiny millimetre lines. 2. Measure 4 things: a fingernail, a pencil, a matchbox and a leaf.
flow.say: The big numbers are centimetres. Between each number there are 10 tiny marks. Each tiny mark is a millimetre. Ten millimetres make one centimetre.
flow.kid: Find the 0 on your ruler. Find the big numbers. They are centimetres. Count the tiny marks between 1 and 2. There are 10. Each is a millimetre.

ask.q: Your pencil reaches 2 tiny marks past the 14. How long is it?

flow.parent: Many children start measuring from the end of the ruler, not the 0. Show that some rulers have a gap before the 0.
flow.context: This is the first step of the paper-strip growth chart. You learn to measure carefully with a ruler, then make a chart of a plant's growth out of paper strips.

check.q: A leaf starts at the 0 and ends exactly on the 6. How long is it?
check.why: The big numbered lines are centimetres. So a leaf that ends at the 6 is 6 centimetres long. That is the same as 60 millimetres. Picking '6 millimetres' usually means mixing up the big lines and the tiny marks.

flow.do: 1. Measure the plant from the soil to its top. 2. Cut a paper strip exactly as long as the plant. 3. Stick it at the left of the big sheet, standing up, with its bottom on a line. 4. Write the date and height under it.
flow.say: This strip is exactly as tall as our plant today. Tomorrow we'll cut another one.
flow.kid: Measure your plant. Cut a paper strip just as long. Stick it on the big sheet. Write the date and the number under it.

flow.do: Each day at the same time, measure again, cut a new strip and stick it beside the last one.
flow.say: Same time every day, so it's fair.
flow.kid: Same time every day. Measure. Cut a strip. Stick it next to yesterday's.

flow.do: After 10 strips, look at the chart together. Find the day it grew most, by finding the biggest jump between two strips.
flow.say: Our strips have made a chart. Look for the biggest jump from one strip to the next. That was the day it grew most.
flow.kid: Look at your strips. They make a chart! Find the biggest jump. That day, your plant grew most.

ask.q: How much did it grow on its best day?
good: Take yesterday's height away from today's.

ask.q: Did it grow the same amount every day?
good: No, some days more, some days less.

flow.parent: This paper chart is a real bar chart. Each strip is a bar. Children who make one usually understand bar charts straight away.
flow.think: Was the weather different on the day it grew most? Warmer? Sunnier?

activities.context: This activity teaches careful measuring with a ruler. Then you cut a paper strip as tall as your plant every day. Stuck side by side, the strips make a growth chart.

activities.title: Plant Doctor: which need is missing?

materials.item: 5 or more plants at home, on the balcony, in your building or at a neighbour's
a notebook and pencil
a magnifying glass, if you have one

activities.safety: Ask the owner before touching anyone else's plant. Wash your hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Examine 5 plants, write a diagnosis and a cure for each, and check them again in a week.

activities.record: For each plant, write: the clue, the missing need, and the cure.

flow.do: Show your child the clue chart below and read it together.
flow.say: A plant can't talk. But it shows us clues. Tall, pale and leaning means it needs light. Drooping with dry soil means water. Yellow with soggy, smelly soil means too much water. Roots coming out of the hole means it needs a bigger pot.
flow.kid: A plant can't talk, but it gives clues. Tall, pale, leaning: it needs light. Droopy, dry soil: it needs water. Yellow, soggy soil: too much water.
flow.context: This is the first step of Plant Doctor. You examine real plants for clues and work out which need is missing.

chart.title: The plant doctor's clue chart
rows: Tall, thin, pale, leaning one way
Yellow leaves, soil soggy or smelly
Air for the roots (too much water)
Water less, check the drainage hole
Roots coming out of the hole
Move it to a bigger pot
Brown, crispy leaf edges in summer sun

flow.do: Visit 5 plants. For each, check: leaves, stem, soil (press a finger in), the hole at the bottom of the pot, and which way it leans. Write a diagnosis and a cure.
flow.say: Be a plant doctor. Look, touch the soil and check the pot. Which need is missing?
flow.kid: Look at 5 plants. Check the leaves. Feel the soil. Look at the pot's hole. Which need is missing? Write it down.

ask.q: What clue told you that?
good: It was leaning towards the window.
Its leaves were droopy and the soil was dry.

flow.parent: Many home plants show more than one clue. That's normal. Ask: which clue is the strongest? Ask the owner before doing a cure.

flow.do: Choose one plant to help, with the owner's permission. Do the cure. Look again in a week.
flow.say: Let's help one plant. Then we'll see if our diagnosis was right.
flow.kid: Choose one plant to help. Do the cure. Look again in a week. Was your diagnosis right?

check.q: A money plant in a dark corridor has long gaps between its leaves and leans towards the door. Which need is missing?
check.why: Long gaps between leaves and leaning are clues of too little light. The plant is stretching towards the brightest place. Picking 'water' is common, because many sick plants need water. But a thirsty plant droops and its soil is dry.

activities.context: This is the plant doctor activity. You read the clues a real plant gives you, like drooping, yellowing or leaning, and work out which need is missing.

activities.title: The Light Map of Our Home

materials.item: a sheet of paper to draw a simple map of your home
a phone with a free light-meter app, if you have one
a white sheet of paper and a pencil, for the shadow test

activities.safety: Never look straight at the Sun, even for a moment.

schedule.what: Measure or test the light in 6 places at home. Mark them on a map. Decide where each plant should live.

activities.record: A map of your home with the brightest and darkest places marked, and where each plant should go.

flow.do: Draw a quick map of your home together: rooms, windows, the balcony and the doors.
flow.say: Let's make a map of how bright each place in our home is. Plants can't walk to the light, so we have to choose for them.
flow.kid: Draw a map of your home. Show the rooms, the windows and the balcony.
flow.context: This is the first step of the light map. You find out how bright different places in your home are, and choose where each plant should live.

flow.do: Visit 6 places: next to a sunny window, the middle of a room, a corridor, a bathroom, the balcony, and outside. In each place, use the light-meter app. Or hold a pencil over white paper and see how dark and sharp its shadow is.
flow.say: Our eyes are tricky. They adjust, so a room feels bright even when it is much dimmer than outside. A light meter tells the truth.
flow.kid: Go to 6 places. Measure the light with the app. Or look at a pencil's shadow. A dark, sharp shadow means bright light.

ask.q: Which place is brightest? Which is darkest?

flow.parent: Light meters measure in lux. Outdoor daylight is often tens of thousands of lux. A bright room is often a few hundred. So a room can be a hundred times dimmer than outside, even though it does not feel like it. That is why indoor plants lean to the windows.

flow.do: Mark each place on the map: very bright, bright, dim or dark. Then decide where your home's plants should live.
flow.say: A tulsi needs lots of sun. A money plant is happy with less. Where should each of our plants go?
flow.kid: Colour each place on the map: very bright, bright, dim or dark. Draw where each plant should live.

check.q: Outside on a sunny day and in the middle of a room, which is usually brighter, and by how much?
options: About the same, because the room feels bright
Outside, often about a hundred times brighter or more
check.why: Our eyes adjust to dim light, so a room feels bright. But a light meter shows that outside daylight is often a hundred times brighter, or more. Picking 'about the same' means trusting our eyes, which is what nearly everyone does. Plants are not fooled.

flow.think: Your eyes adjusted so well that you did not notice how dim the room was. What else might your senses be hiding from you?

activities.context: This activity maps how bright each place in your home is, using a light-meter app or shadows. Then you choose the best place for each plant.

activities.title: Bose's Growth Magnifier

materials.item: a fast-growing young plant, such as a bean, gourd or moong seedling at least 10 cm tall
a long plastic straw, about 20 cm
a pin and a small lump of clay or a cork, on top of a stick or a stack of books
a soft cotton thread about 20 cm long
a small paper clip and a strip of paper marked in centimetres

activities.safety: A grown-up handles the pin. Tie the thread loosely, so it does not cut the plant.

schedule.what: Build the straw lever, connect it to the plant and watch the pointer move over 2 or 3 hours.

activities.record: Write where the pointer was each half hour. Work out how far it moved, and how much the plant really grew.

flow.do: Tell your child about Jagadish Chandra Bose and his crescograph.
flow.say: More than a hundred years ago, in Kolkata, Jagadish Chandra Bose built a special machine. It made a plant's growth look thousands of times bigger. Today we'll build a tiny cousin of it.
flow.kid: Long ago in Kolkata, a scientist called Bose built a machine. It made plant growth look huge. You can see a plant grow! Let's build a small one.
flow.context: This is the first step of Bose's Growth Magnifier. You build a simple straw lever that makes a plant's slow growth easier to see. It is a tiny version of Jagadish Chandra Bose's crescograph.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up pushes the pin through the straw about 4 cm from one end. 2. Push the pin into the clay or cork on top of the stick, so the straw can swing like a seesaw. 3. Hang the paper clip on the long end, so it tips down. 4. Tie one end of the thread loosely around the plant's top, just below the growing tip. 5. Tie the other end to the short end of the straw, so the thread is straight and tight. 6. Stand the paper scale behind the long end of the straw.
flow.say: The short end is 4 centimetres from the pin. The long end is about 16 centimetres. So when the plant grows a little, the long end moves 4 times as far.
flow.kid: With a grown-up, push a pin through the straw near one end. Balance it on clay. Tie the short end to the plant's top with thread. The long end is your pointer.
flow.parent: The paper clip makes the long end heavier, so the short end always pulls the thread tight. As the plant grows up, the thread loosens, the short end rises, and the long end drops along the scale.

flow.do: Mark where the pointer is now. Then mark it every half hour for 2 to 3 hours.
flow.say: Let's mark the pointer every half hour. Is the plant growing right now, while we watch?
flow.kid: Mark where the pointer is. Look again every half hour. Mark it again. Is it moving?
flow.wait: Check every 30 minutes for 2 or 3 hours.
flow.parent: A young bean shoot can grow a millimetre or more each hour on a warm day. With this lever, the pointer moves about 4 millimetres for every millimetre of growth. If nothing moves, check that the thread is still tight.

flow.do: Work out how much the plant really grew: the pointer moved 4 times as far as the plant grew.
flow.say: The pointer moved 12 millimetres. The lever makes it look 4 times bigger. So how much did the plant really grow?
flow.kid: Measure how far the pointer moved. The plant grew 4 times less. Work it out.

ask.q: If the pointer moved 12 millimetres, how much did the plant grow?

check.q: The pointer on the long end of the straw moved 8 millimetres. The long end moves 4 times as far as the plant grows. How much did the plant grow?
check.why: The lever makes growth look 4 times bigger. So the real growth is 8 divided by 4, which is 2 millimetres. Picking '32' means multiplying instead of dividing: the plant's growth is the small number, not the big one.

flow.think: Bose's machine made growth look ten thousand times bigger. He saw it speed up and slow down from minute to minute. What could make a plant grow faster for a few minutes?

activities.context: This activity builds a simple straw lever that makes a plant's growth easier to see. It is a tiny version of the crescograph, a growth-measuring machine invented by Jagadish Chandra Bose in Kolkata.

activities.title: Seedling Dance: in the dark and in the light

materials.item: a torch, or a window with sunlight
some space to move

activities.safety: Move gently and keep away from furniture edges.

schedule.what: Act out seedlings growing in the dark, in the light, in too much water and in the cold and heat.

activities.record: Draw yourself as a seedling in the dark and in the light.

flow.do: Ask your child to curl up small on the floor like a seed in the soil.
flow.say: You're a moong seed in the soil. Curl up tight. You have a packed lunch inside you.
flow.kid: Curl up small like a seed. You have a little packed lunch inside you.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Seedling Dance. You act out how a seedling grows in the light, in the dark, and in too much water, cold and heat.

flow.do: Turn off the lights. Ask your child to grow like a seedling in the dark.
flow.say: It's dark. You can't make food. Stretch up as tall and thin as you can, fast, looking for light. Keep your hands folded shut, like small closed leaves.
flow.kid: It is dark. Stretch up tall and thin, fast. Keep your hands folded. You are looking for light!

ask.q: How does it feel to stretch and stretch?

flow.do: Shine the torch, or open the curtains. Ask your child to grow like a seedling in the light.
flow.say: Light! Now open your leaves wide, like hands catching sunshine. Stand strong and solid. You don't need to stretch so far.
flow.kid: Light! Open your hands wide like leaves. Stand strong. Turn your face to the light.
flow.think: Which seedling felt stronger: the one in the dark, or the one in the light?

flow.do: Call out other conditions and let your child act each one: soggy soil, a cold night, a heat wave, just right.
flow.say: Soggy soil! Your roots can't breathe. A cold night, 5 degrees! A heat wave, 46 degrees! Now everything is just right.
flow.kid: Act it out! Soggy soil. A cold night. A heat wave. Now everything is just right.

check.q: In the dance, a seedling in the dark stretches tall and keeps its leaves shut. Why?
options: It is using its stored food to reach light, and leaves are no use without light
check.why: Without light, leaves cannot make food. So a seedling in the dark spends its stored food on stretching up, not on opening leaves. Picking 'cold' mixes up two needs. A seedling in the cold hardly grows at all.

activities.context: This is a movement activity. Your child acts out a seedling growing in the dark and in the light, and in soggy, cold and hot conditions. It comes from the founder's idea of a dance of sunbeams and plants.

projects.title: My Bean, My Diary

materials.item: a pot about 15 cm across, with a hole in the bottom
soil mixed with a handful of compost
3 rajma, lobia or broad bean seeds, soaked overnight
a stick about 60 cm long for the bean to climb
a ruler, a thermometer if you have one, and a notebook

projects.safety: Wash hands after touching soil and compost. Do not eat raw rajma seeds, because they are harmful uncooked.

schedule.what: Choose the best place using your light map. Sow the beans. Name your plant. Start the diary.
Check the soil with a finger. Water if dry. Write one line in the diary.
Measure the shoot. Write the height, the weather and the temperature.
Measure. Push in the stick for climbing.
Measure. Count the leaves. Do a plant doctor check.
Measure. Draw the plant.
Measure. Did anything slow it down?
Final measuring. Draw a growth chart of all your measurements. Write what helped and what harmed your plant. Show your diary to the family.

projects.record: A diary with a page every third day: date, height, number of leaves, weather, temperature and one sentence about how the plant looks. At the end, a bar chart of the heights.

flow.do: Look at the light map from the light map activity, if you made one. Choose a bright place with some morning sun for the pot.
flow.say: Beans need lots of light, water that is just right, and warmth. Where in our home is the best place?
flow.kid: Look at your light map. Find a bright place with some morning sun. That is your bean's home.
flow.context: This is the first step of My Bean, My Diary. You grow a bean plant for three weeks, look after all its needs and keep a diary of its growth.

flow.do: 1. Fill the pot with the soil and compost. 2. Push 3 soaked beans in, about 2 cm deep and a hand-width apart. 3. Water until a little runs out of the hole. 4. Give your plant a name and write it on the pot.
flow.say: Some families talk to their plant and name it. Let's name ours. What will you call your bean?
flow.kid: Fill the pot. Push in 3 beans, 2 cm deep. Water until a little runs out of the hole. Give your plant a name!
flow.parent: Naming the plant is the founder's idea. Children care for a plant they have named. If more than one bean comes up, keep the strongest and gently pull out the others after a week, so it has space.

flow.do: Every third day: 1. Press a finger into the soil. Water only if the top is dry. 2. Measure the shoot from the soil to the tip. 3. Write the height, the number of leaves, the weather and the temperature in the diary.
flow.say: Check first, then water. Too much water drowns the roots. Then measure and write it down.
flow.kid: Every third day: feel the soil. Water only if it is dry. Measure your bean. Write it in your diary.

check.q: You press your finger into the bean's soil and it feels damp. What should you do?
options: Water it anyway, because more water is better
check.why: Damp soil already has enough water. Watering again could make it soggy, so the roots cannot get air. Picking 'water it anyway' is the most common mistake in looking after plants. Checking first is what good gardeners do.

flow.do: When the bean is about 15 cm tall, push the stick into the soil beside it, without hurting the roots.
flow.say: Beans are climbers. Watch what the tip does with the stick in the next few days.
flow.kid: Push a stick into the soil next to your bean. Watch the tip. Will it find the stick?
flow.think: The bean has no eyes. How does it find the stick to climb?

flow.do: On Day 21: 1. Measure one last time. 2. Make a bar chart with one bar for each measuring day. 3. Write two sentences: what helped your plant grow and what slowed it down. 4. Show the diary to the family.
flow.say: Look at your chart. When did it grow fastest? Was the weather different then? What would you change next time?
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each day you measured. When did your bean grow fastest? Write what helped it and what slowed it down.

chart.title: Made-up example: my bean's height every third day
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your bean will be different.

flow.parent: If the plant dies, that is a real result too. Be a plant doctor together: which need was missing? The founder suggests writing a short note about how it feels to lose a plant, and then trying again.

challenges.title: Light for a Dark Corner
challenges.problem: A plant has to live in a dim corner, a few steps from the window. It is leaning and pale. Your job is to get more light to it without moving the pot.
constraints: Use only things from home, like white paper, cardboard, steel plates, mirrors and kitchen foil.
materials: a plant or a cup of seedlings in a dim corner
white paper, cardboard and sticky tape
kitchen foil, a steel thali or a small mirror
a light-meter app, or a pencil and white paper for the shadow test
general: Put white card or kitchen foil behind and beside the plant, so light that falls there bounces back onto the leaves.
Clean the window. A dusty window can block a lot of light.
Open the curtains wider, or tie them back.
creative: Use a steel thali or a mirror outside the window to bounce a patch of sunlight into the room. Move it every hour to follow the Sun.
Make a light funnel: line a cardboard tube with foil and point one end at the window and the other at the plant.
In some old houses in India, a small glass tile in the roof let daylight into a dark room. Could a 'skylight' of foil-lined card work for you?
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way. Draw it, build it and measure the light before and after. Which idea gave the most light?

flow.do: Measure how bright the dim corner is now, with a light-meter app or the pencil-shadow test.
flow.say: First, let's measure how dark it is now, so we know if our ideas really help.
flow.kid: Measure how bright the corner is now. Use the app, or look at a pencil's shadow on white paper.
flow.context: This is the first step of Light for a Dark Corner. A plant in a dim corner needs more light, and you must bring the light to the plant without moving it.

flow.do: Before trying anything, draw or list three ideas together.
flow.say: Engineers think before they build. Let's list three ideas.
flow.kid: Think like an engineer. Draw three ideas to bring light to the corner.

flow.do: Try each idea, one at a time, and measure the light at the plant after each one.
flow.say: Try one idea at a time. Measure after each one. That's a fair test of our ideas.
flow.kid: Try your ideas one at a time. Measure the light after each one. Which works best?
flow.parent: Foil and white card usually help a little. A mirror or thali bouncing direct sunlight can help a lot, but only while the Sun is in the right place. Never point reflected sunlight at anyone's eyes.

check.q: You try foil and a clean window at the same time, and the light gets brighter. Which idea worked?
options: You can't tell, because you changed two things at once
check.why: Two things changed, so you cannot tell which one helped, or how much. Try one idea, measure, then add the next. Picking 'the foil' or 'the window' means guessing. A fair test of your ideas changes only one thing at a time.

flow.do: Read the usual solutions and the creative ideas. Then invent one more.
flow.say: Here's what people usually do, and some creative ideas. Can you invent something new?
flow.kid: Look at the usual ways and the creative ideas. Now invent your own way.
flow.think: People in a crowded city also live in dim rooms. How do light and sunlight change how people feel?

challenges.title: The Holiday Waterer
challenges.problem: Your family is going away for 7 days. Your plant must have water that is just right the whole time: not dry, and not soaked. Design a way to water it while you are away.
constraints: Nobody can visit the plant for 7 days.
The soil must not get soggy, because roots need air.
materials: a potted plant, or a cup of seedlings
plastic bottles, cotton string or a strip of old cloth, a small clay pot or matka if you have one
a nail for a grown-up to make small holes
general: Fill a plastic bottle with water, make a tiny hole in the cap, and push it upside down into the soil. It drips slowly.
Put a jug of water beside the pot. Bury one end of a cotton string in the soil and put the other end in the water. The string soaks up water and carries it to the soil, a little at a time.
Move the plant to a shadier, cooler place, so it loses less water while you are away.
creative: Bury a small unglazed clay pot full of water in a big pot of soil, with its mouth just above the soil. Water seeps slowly through the clay. Farmers in India and many other places have watered plants with buried clay pots for a very long time.
Put the plant in a clear plastic bag, loosely, like a tiny greenhouse. The water it breathes out drips back into the soil. Do not seal it tight, and keep it out of direct sun.
Group all your plants together on a tray of damp pebbles. They keep each other's air moist.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way. Test it for 3 days before your trip and check the soil each day. Is it dry, damp or soggy?

flow.do: Read the problem together. Ask: what does just-right water mean for this plant?
flow.say: We need to give the plant water slowly, a little every day. Too much at once, and the roots drown.
flow.kid: Your plant needs water for 7 days while you are away. Not too little. Not too much. How could you do it?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Holiday Waterer. It is an engineering challenge: keep a plant's water just right for 7 days with nobody at home.

flow.do: Draw three ideas together. Then build the one your child likes best.
flow.say: Let's draw three ideas, then build the best one.
flow.kid: Draw three ideas. Then build the best one. Ask a grown-up for help with holes.

flow.do: Test the waterer on the plant for 3 days. Check the soil each day with a finger and write: dry, damp or soggy.
flow.say: A good engineer tests before the trip. Let's check the soil every day.
flow.kid: Test your waterer for 3 days. Feel the soil each day. Dry, damp or soggy? Write it down.
flow.wait: Check the soil once a day for 3 days.

flow.do: Look at the results. Fix the design if the soil was dry or soggy, and test it again.
flow.say: Was the soil just right every day? If not, what will you change?
flow.kid: Was the soil just right? If it was dry, give more water. If it was soggy, give less. Fix it and test again.

check.q: Your bottle waterer made the soil soggy by the second day. What should you change?
options: Make the hole in the cap bigger
Make the hole smaller, so the water comes out more slowly
check.why: Soggy soil means water is coming in faster than the plant uses it. A smaller hole slows the drip. Picking 'bigger hole' or 'bigger bottle' gives even more water. Remember, roots need air too.

flow.do: Read the usual and creative solutions. Then invent one more, and choose the one to use on your real trip.
flow.say: Here's what people usually do, and some clever old ideas. Which will we use for the real trip?
flow.kid: Look at the usual ways and the creative ideas. Can you invent a better one?
flow.think: The buried clay pot idea is very old. Why do you think people kept using it for so long?
