quiz.p: Which list shows what a plant needs to grow well?
opts: Light, water, air, warmth and minerals
quiz.why: Plants need light, water, air, warmth and minerals. Picking 'only soil and water' leaves out light, which plants use to make food.

opts: You change only one thing and keep everything else the same
quiz.why: Changing only one thing tells you what caused the result. Picking 'test only one plant' misses that one plant can be a fluke.

quiz.p: In the light test, you forget to water the dark cups. What is wrong with the test?
opts: Two things changed, light and water, so you can't tell which caused the result
quiz.why: A fair test changes only one thing. Picking 'nothing' means noticing the planned change but not the accidental one.
quiz.context: This question is about the light test. You grow moong seedlings in 6 cups. Three get light and three are kept under a box, with everything else the same.

quiz.p: Where does the 0 on the ruler go when you measure a plant's height?
opts: At the top of the cup
At the top of the plant
quiz.why: Height is measured from the soil up. Picking 'top of the cup' leaves out the part of the stem inside the cup.

quiz.p: A seedling is 6 centimetres and 5 millimetres tall. How many millimetres is that?
quiz.why: Each centimetre is 10 millimetres. So 6 centimetres is 60 millimetres, and 5 more makes 65. Picking 11 means adding 6 and 5 without changing the units.

quiz.p: Look at the chart. Which cup's seedlings grew taller?
quiz.why: The DARK bar is taller: 14 cm against 8 cm. But remember, the dark ones were pale and weak. Picking LIGHT means answering 'which was healthier' instead of 'which was taller'.
quiz.context: This question is about the light test. You grow moong seedlings in 6 cups. Three get light and three are kept under a box, with everything else the same.

chart.title: The light test: middle height on Day 7 (made-up results)

quiz.p: Which sentence is a good conclusion for the water test?
opts: We found that the JUST RIGHT seedlings grew tallest, at 13 cm. This shows moong needs some water, but not too much.
quiz.why: A good conclusion says what was found, uses a number as proof, and says what it shows. Picking 'I watered the plants' describes what you did, not what you found.
quiz.context: This question is about the water test. Three cups of moong get no water. Three get 2 teaspoons every second day. Three stand in a dish of water all the time.

quiz.p: A plant is tall, thin, pale and leaning towards the window. Which need is missing?
quiz.why: Leaning and pale are clues of too little light. Picking 'water' is common, but thirsty plants droop in dry soil.

quiz.p: A plant has yellow leaves and its soil is always soggy and smells bad. What is wrong?
opts: Too much water, so the roots can't get air
quiz.why: Soggy soil drowns the roots. Picking 'too little water' is the opposite mistake, because yellow leaves can come from both.

quiz.p: Is more water always better for a plant?
opts: No. Roots need air too, and soaked soil drowns them
quiz.why: Each need must be just right. Picking 'yes' is one of the most common mistakes in caring for plants.

quiz.p: Which is true about warmth and plants?
opts: The hotter, the faster they grow, with no limit
Warmth speeds up growth, but too much heat harms plants
Plants grow fastest in the fridge
quiz.why: Each plant has a just-right range. Picking 'no limit' misses that great heat harms the plant's helper molecules.

quiz.p: Why is wheat sown in the cool winter in Punjab?
opts: Wheat grows best in cool weather
quiz.why: Each crop has its own just right. Wheat likes it cool. Picking 'a flooded field' describes rice, not wheat.

quiz.p: How does a seedling in the dark sense that it is dark?
opts: With tiny eyes on its leaves
With special light-sensing molecules, such as phytochrome
quiz.why: Plants have photoreceptor molecules that change in light. Picking 'eyes' gives plants an animal body part they don't have.

quiz.p: Astronauts on the International Space Station ate lettuce they had grown there. When?
opts: Nobody has grown food in space
quiz.why: The Veggie garden grew red lettuce that astronauts ate in August 2015. Picking 1969 mixes it up with the first Moon landing.

quiz.p: Who built the crescograph, a machine that showed a plant growing minute by minute?
quiz.why: Bose built it in Kolkata. Picking Newton is a guess based on a famous name.

applications: Farmers sow each crop in the season whose warmth and rain suit it. Rabi wheat is sown in winter, and kharif rice in the monsoon.
Greenhouses and polyhouses keep plants warm and protected, so farmers can grow vegetables out of season.
Drip irrigation gives each plant just the right water, drop by drop, and saves a lot of water. Many Indian farms use it.
Plant nurseries put sun-loving plants in full sun and shade-loving plants under green shade nets.
Hydroponic farms on city rooftops grow lettuce, spinach and herbs in mineral water with no soil.
Grow lights in vertical farms and space gardens use red and blue lamps, the colours plants use most.
Seed banks keep seeds cold and dry so they stay alive for many years.
Fair tests are used by scientists who breed new crops, to find out which kind grows best in heat or drought.
Weather forecasts help farmers decide when to sow and when to water.
Space agencies are testing how to grow food for long journeys to the Moon and Mars.
Gardeners use pots with drainage holes and add sand to heavy soil, so roots get air.
Botanic gardens keep plants from deserts, rainforests and mountains alive by copying the light, water and warmth of their homes.

open_questions.q: Exactly how does a plant feel warmth?
open_questions.why_open: In 2016 scientists found that a light-sensing molecule, phytochrome B, also senses warmth. Since then they have found other warmth-sensing molecules. How they all work together is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: Why does a plant's growth speed up and slow down from minute to minute?
open_questions.why_open: Jagadish Chandra Bose saw this with his crescograph over a hundred years ago. Scientists now know many signals are involved, from light and warmth to water and the plant's own daily clock. But the whole picture is still not clear.

open_questions.q: How will India's crops cope as summers get hotter?
open_questions.why_open: Early heat waves have already shrunk wheat harvests. Scientists are breeding crops that cope better with heat, but nobody knows yet how well they will keep up.

open_questions.q: Could we grow food in the soil of the Moon or Mars?
open_questions.why_open: In 2022, small plants grew in real Moon soil, but slowly and stressed. Mars soil contains harmful salts. Scientists are still testing ways to make these soils safe for plants.

open_questions.q: Do plants respond to sound in useful ways?
open_questions.why_open: Some experiments show plants react to the vibrations of chewing insects, or of running water. Others find nothing. It is hard to test fairly, and scientists still argue.

open_questions.q: How does a seedling decide how to share its packed lunch between roots, stem and leaves?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that light, water and minerals all change the decision, through plant hormones. How a plant without a brain balances all of these is still being studied.

maths.problem: In the light test, a seedling was 3 cm tall on Day 3 and 8 cm tall on Day 7. How much did it grow between Day 3 and Day 7?
maths.explain: The seedling was 8 cm on Day 7 and 3 cm on Day 3. 8 take away 3 is 5. So it grew 5 cm. You can check: 3 + 5 = 8.
maths.context: This question is about the light test. You grow moong seedlings in 6 cups. Three get light and three are kept under a box, with everything else the same.
maths.why_maths: A ruler tells you how tall a plant is. Taking away yesterday's height from today's tells you how much it grew, which is what we really want to know.

maths.problem: Look at the ruler in the picture. The top of a seedling is at the arrow, halfway between 6 and 7. Each big number is a centimetre. How tall is the seedling, in centimetres and in millimetres?
maths.answer: 6 and a half centimetres, which is 65 millimetres.
maths.explain: The arrow is past the 6, halfway to the 7. Halfway is 5 tiny millimetre marks. So the seedling is 6 centimetres and 5 millimetres. Each centimetre is 10 millimetres, so 6 centimetres is 60 millimetres. 60 + 5 = 65 millimetres.
maths.context: In this unit you measure seedlings with a ruler every day. The big numbers on a ruler are centimetres. The tiny marks between them are millimetres. Ten millimetres make one centimetre.

chart.title: A ruler, measuring in centimetres
chart.label: Each tiny mark is 1 millimetre. Halfway between two numbers is 5 millimetres.

maths.why_maths: Seedlings grow only a few millimetres a day. Reading the tiny marks on a ruler lets you see growth that whole centimetres would miss.

maths.problem: In the warmth test, you put a thermometer in each place. Look at the thermometer in the picture. What temperature does it show?
maths.explain: The red line stops at the mark 2 above the 25. Each mark is 1 degree. So the temperature is 25 + 2 = 27 degrees Celsius. That is the temperature of the room cupboard.
maths.context: This question is about the warmth test. Moong sprouts are kept in the dark in a fridge, a room cupboard and a warm spot, and measured each day.

chart.title: A room thermometer, in degrees Celsius (°C)
chart.label: Each small mark is 1 degree.

maths.why_maths: To know if warmth changes growth, you must know how warm each place really was. A thermometer only helps if you can read it.

maths.problem: Look at the bar chart from the water test. How much taller was the JUST RIGHT group than the SOAKED group?
maths.explain: The JUST RIGHT bar reaches 13 cm and the SOAKED bar reaches 8 cm. 13 take away 8 is 5. So the JUST RIGHT seedlings were 5 cm taller.
maths.context: This question is about the water test. Three cups of moong get no water. Three get 2 teaspoons every second day. Three stand in a dish of water all the time.

chart.title: The water test: middle height on Day 14 (made-up results)

maths.why_maths: After a test you have a list of numbers. A bar chart shows the best group at a glance, and reading two bars tells you how big the difference is.

maths.problem: In the light test, the three DARK cups measured 13 cm, 15 cm and 14 cm. What is the middle value?
maths.explain: Put the numbers in order: 13, 14, 15. The one in the middle is 14. So the middle value is 14 cm.
maths.context: This question is about the light test. You grow moong seedlings in 6 cups. Three get light and three are kept under a box, with everything else the same.
maths.why_maths: Three cups never give exactly the same number. The middle value gives one fair number for the group, and stops one odd cup from fooling us.

maths.problem: In the warmth test, the 5 longest sprouts in the warm bowl added up to 6 cm on Day 1. On Day 4 they added up to 30 cm. How much did they grow? How much is that for each sprout, on average?
maths.answer: They grew 24 cm altogether. That is about 4 cm for each of the 5 sprouts, and a little more.
maths.explain: 30 take away 6 is 24. So the 5 sprouts grew 24 cm altogether. 24 shared between 5 sprouts is 4, with 4 cm left over. So each sprout grew a bit more than 4 cm.
maths.context: This question is about the warmth test. Moong sprouts are kept in the dark in a fridge, a room cupboard and a warm spot, and measured each day.
maths.why_maths: Adding up 5 sprouts gives one number for each bowl. Sharing it back out tells you how much a single sprout grew.

roots.context: We have been learning what a plant needs, using fair tests of light, water and warmth. Now we ask what a plant's needs tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: No living thing is self-made. Each one is held up by sun, water, air and soil.
deep_truth.habit: We call a plant independent because it makes its own food. But it needs light from a star 150 million kilometres away.
deep_truth.evidence: A seedling in the dark grows pale and weak.

three.who_am_i: Like a plant, you need light, water, air and warmth to grow.
three.what_is_life: Too little is bad, and too much is bad too. Life needs just enough.
three.what_is_this_world: The light that grows your food left the Sun eight minutes before.

roots.thread: A moong seedling needs light from a star, water from clouds, air shared by everyone and minerals from old rocks. It cannot grow from any one thing alone. DeepKids believes the One shows up in this: every living thing is held by the whole world. A plant is the Sun, the rain and the soil, gathered into one.

teachings.source: Samyutta Nikaya 56.11, the Buddha's first teaching
teachings.teaching: The Buddha taught a middle path. Not too much, and not too little.
teachings.link: A plant needs water, light and warmth in the right amount. Too much water drowns its roots. Too little dries it.

teachings.teaching: From space came air. From air came fire, and from fire, water. From water came earth, and from earth, plants.
teachings.link: A plant gathers air, warmth, water and earth into one living thing. It needs all of them.

science.text: A plant's growth is held back by whatever it has least of. This is a useful rule, though real plants are more complicated.
Sunlight takes about eight minutes to travel from the Sun to a leaf.

other_view.view: Jains teach that each plant has its own soul, separate from every other soul. On this view, the world is many separate living beings, not one.

practice.title: Sun and shade
practice.say: Let's stand in a patch of sunlight for one minute. Close your eyes and feel the warmth on your face and arms. Then step into the shade and stand still for one minute. Breathe slowly. What changed on your skin? A plant feels this difference too, in its own way.
practice.kid: Stand in the sun. Close your eyes. Feel the warmth. Then step into the shade. What changed?
